beliefs.practice: Read the cluster connection string only from environment (process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI) or from Key Vault at runtime; never hard-code it into source, logs, README, or test fixtures and provide only a .env.example with a placeholder.

Always connect with TLS/SSL enabled and certificate validation (do not disable tls or tlsAllowInvalidCertificates); ensure your Mongo client URI uses tls=true (or the equivalent) so all traffic to the DocumentDB cluster is encrypted.

Tune Mongo/Mongoose connection options: set maxPoolSize to a value appropriate for the VM (e.g., 50–200 per process), serverSelectionTimeoutMS (e.g., 30000), and socketTimeoutMS (e.g., 120000) to avoid long blocking when the cluster is transiently unreachable.

Use a single shared Mongoose connection per process (reuse the mongoose connection across modules) rather than creating many short-lived connections; size the pool instead of spinning up more processes to avoid connection storms.

When scanning all active accounts, use a server cursor with pagination (find().batchSize(500) / cursor.each or async iteration) and projection to return only fields needed for interest calculation (e.g., _id, balance, rate, status) to limit memory and RU consumption.
Avoid skip-based pagination for large scans; use range-based pagination (e.g., sort by _id or lastModified and use > lastSeenId) or an explicit cursor so each batch is efficient and repeatable.

Write journal entries with unordered bulkWrite({ ordered: false }) in moderate batches (commonly 200–1000 ops per batch) to maximize throughput while avoiding huge single requests that spike RU and risk partial failures.

Enforce idempotency by creating a unique compound index on the journal collection (e.g., { accountId: 1, accrualDate: 1 }) so repeated accrual runs produce duplicate-key errors you can detect and ignore.

Create an index tuned for the scanning query on accounts: a partial or filtered index that only indexes active interest-bearing accounts (e.g., partialFilterExpression: { status: 'active', interestEnabled: true } and include fields used in projection) to reduce RU and I/O.

Handle transient rate-limiting (HTTP 429 / Mongo mapped throttling) by reading the server Retry-After/Retry-After-ms where available, implementing exponential backoff with jitter, and consider reducing batch size or increasing RU/s when 429s are frequent.

Treat bulkWrite partial failures as normal: inspect bulkWriteResult and writeErrors, retry only idempotent operations (or those that failed due to transient errors) and suppress duplicate-key errors (11000) when enforcing idempotency via unique index.

Create indexes at deployment/migration time idempotently (createIndex with background where supported), and verify index existence before producing large scans; do not rely on implicit index creation at runtime during high-load jobs.

Monitor RU/s, RU consumption per operation, request charge on queries, and 429 counts in metrics and set alerts (e.g., when RU% > 70% or 429s increase) so you can scale RU or reduce batch sizes before jobs start failing.

Store accrual timestamps in UTC (ISO 8601) and use a single canonical accrualDate key used by the unique index so different processes/runs compute the same journal key and idempotency works across time zones.

Keep journal documents immutable (never update an accrual document) and, if retention is required, use a TTL index (expireAfterSeconds) on the journal collection rather than updating/removing documents frequently.

When reading accounts for computation, use projection and lean() (Mongoose) to avoid full Mongoose document overhead; e.g., Account.find(query).select('balance rate _id').lean().cursor().batchSize(500).
Cap batch sizes and add short pauses between bulkWrite batches (micro-sleeps or yield) if you observe RU spikes or 429 throttling from the cluster to smooth throughput for scheduled daily jobs.

Do not rely on multi-document transactions for high-throughput archival/journal workloads; prefer idempotent single-document writes and unique constraints. If transactions are required, test support on the target server version before using them in production.

Limit document size and the amount of indexed data per document (avoid wide documents) so reads/writes consume fewer RUs and indexes remain small; keep accrual journal entries compact (only accountId, accrualDate, amount, metadata).
Store and rotate production credentials in Azure Key Vault and use short-lived credentials or rotate primary keys regularly; do not commit primary keys into repos or CI logs.

When working with vector-capable clusters, keep vector index parameter tuning out of hot paths: configure HNSW / DiskANN parameters (M, efConstruction, index type) at index creation time and set ef (efSearch) per query to trade recall/latency; avoid creating vector indexes with overly large construction params during daily jobs.

Include unit and integration tests that run the accrual worker against a local or test cluster with a seeded dataset (verify idempotency, duplicate-key handling, and bulkWrite partial failure handling), and mock or assert Retry-After behavior for transient failures.
